Synthesis of 1,4-Allenyne and 1,5-Enyne Thioaryl Carboxylates

ABSTRACT: The first Doyle−Kirmse reaction on alkynyl diazoacetates using allyl/propargyl sulfides is reported. The development
provides diversified 1,5-enyne and 1,4-allenyne thioaryl carboxylates in good yields under ligand-/additive-free AuCl and Rh
2
(OAc)
4
catalysis, respectively (48 examples, up to 96% yield). The study demonstrated the dual role of allyl sulfide as a ligand and substrate.
Also, we have exemplified various synthetic modifications of the products to showcase the utility of different functional groups.
[2,3]-Sigmatropic rearrangement of sulfonium ylides has
garnered significant interest among the synthetic community
as it constructs C−C and C−S bonds simultaneously and
provides various biologically active molecules (Scheme 1a).
1
The rearrangement of sulfonium ylides generated from diazo
compounds and allyl/propargyl sulfides is popularly known as
the Doyle−Kirmse reaction.
2
This reaction has been studied
on different types of donor,
3
acceptor,
4
and donor−acceptor
5
diazo compounds, and a generalization of the reports is
depicted in Scheme 1b.
6
The donor−acceptor carbenes are of
paramount significance due to their controlled reactivity, high
selectivity, and their ascendancy over the other carbenes to
provide highly functionalized motifs with quaternary centers.
7,8
It is witnessed that the target-oriented synthesis of bioactive
molecules containing quaternary centers is a formidable
challenge in organic synthesis. Remarkably, the sigmatropic
rearrangements contribute to about half the volume of such
C−C bond-forming reactions by overcoming the steric
challenges.
8
From this perspective, the reports on sigmatropic rearrange-
ment of carbene precursors having versatile π-bonds are
relatively scarce. We noticed that [2,3]-sigmatropic rearrange-
ment on alkynyl diazoacetates still remains scarce in the
chemistry of donor−acceptor carbenes. In fact, the reactivity of
alkynyl carbenes is still in its infancy, although they have been
known for the past six decades.
9a
Probably, this could be due
to their tendency to undergo rearrangement and isomer-
ization.
9b
Recently, alkynyl carbene transfer reactions from
donor or donor−donor type diazo compounds have been
successfully witnessed in cyclopropanations
10
as well as Si−
H,
11
B−H,
12
and C−C
13
bond insertion reactions. Also, a
sigmatropic rearrangement reaction emerged through a
decomposition of N-nosylhydrazones.
14

generated in situ by a base-promoted decomposition of
specially protected alkynyl hydrazones.
10−14
On the other
hand, alkynyl carbene transfer reactions of alkynyl diazoace-
tates have merely been limited to cyclopropanations,
15,16
silane
insertions,
16
and a multicomponent reaction
17
(Scheme 1c). In
continuation of our research interest in alkynyl carbene transfer
reactions,
16
herein, we are reporting the Doyle−Kirmse
reaction on alkynyl donor−acceptor carbenes by employing
allyl/propargyl aryl sulfides using transition metal catalysis
(Scheme 1d). The development provides expedient access to
highly functionalized and diversified 1,5-enyne and 1,4-
allenyne thioaryl carboxylates.
We started our optimization studies by using alkynyl
diazoacetate 2a and allyl phenyl sulfide 3a under coinage
metal catalysis at 0 °C (Table 1, entries 1−7).
18
Encouraged
by the success of gold catalysis in carbene transfer reactions,
19
we screened AuCl and its complexes of phosphine, phosphite,
and NHC ligands. Delightfully, an additive- and ligand-free
AuCl catalysis afforded the desired product 4a in superior yield
(76%, entry 3). Next, we screened the prominent Rh
2
(OAc)
4
catalyst, and the reaction afforded the product but with a lower
yield (60%, entry 8). Motivated by the superior yield with
ligand- and additive-free AuCl catalysis, we further optimized
the yield by screening different solvents and observed an
improvement in toluene (81% yield, entries 9−12). Next, we
screened temperature to improve the yield, but a reaction at
ambient temperature did not improve the yield (entry 13).
Finally, we attempted a one-pot synthesis from alkynyl
hydrazone 1a that could bypass the purification of
diazoacetates 2a after a metal-free oxidation with PIDA.
16
A
reaction with hydrazone 1a afforded the desired product 4a;
however, we observed a diminished yield (56%, entry 14).
Delightfully, an improvement in yield (up to 88%) was noticed
with an increased loading (1.0 to 1.5 equiv) of hydrazone 1a
(entries 15−16).
Having the optimized conditions in hand, we executed the
substrate scope by varying the hydrazones 1 and sulfides 3 to
obtain a wide variety of 1,5-enyne thioaryl carboxylates
(Scheme 2). First, we examined the compatibility of the
optimized conditions with the steric factor (methyl to
adamantyl) of the ester group of alkynyl hydrazones.
Delightfully, the reactions afforded the desired products 4a−
4e in good to excellent yields (74−96%). Then, we executed
the alkyne scope by screening various hydrazones derived from
p-, o-, and m-substituted aryl acetylenes. Gratifyingly, the
reactions furnished the corresponding products 4f−4p in
moderate to good yields (60−85%). Further, we extended the
scope by validating the hydrazones derived from naphthyl and
thienyl acetylenes. The reactions furnished the corresponding
products 4q−4s in 62−80% yield. Next, we focused our
attention toward the screening of electronic parameters on the
aryl component of sulfide 3. Electron-donating groups (Me
and OMe) at the p-position afforded 4t−4u in moderate yields
(64−68%), while withdrawing groups (F, Cl, and NO
2
)
delivered the corresponding products 4v−4x in good to
excellent yields (78−90%). We screened o-substituted and
polysubstituted thiols and obtained products 4y−4aa in good
yields (71−81%). We also screened a nonaryl substituted allyl
sulfide and obtained the desired product 4ab in 52% yield,
however, after a longer reaction time. Finally, we executed the
reactions with hydrazones derived from naturally available or
biologically active molecules and observed the products 4ac−
4ad in good yields (80−83%), albeit with poor diastereose-
lectivity (1:1 dr). Further, we screened a hydrazone derived
from oleyl alcohol and observed the product 4ae in 86% yield.
Next, we extended our strategy to obtain 1,4-allenyne
thioaryl carboxylates 6 by switching to propargyl sulfides 5
(Scheme 3). We carried out a brief optimization study and
found that the reactions with the Rh
2
(OAc)
4
catalyst
outperformed that of AuCl.
18
The resultant highly function-
alized 1,4-allenyne thioaryl carboxylate 6a was obtained in 81%
yield under the optimized conditions. We executed a short
substrate scope by validating different hydrazones and aryl
propargyl sulfides. As anticipated, the optimized conditions
were compatible with the steric bulkiness of the ester and
different aryl alkynes of the hydrazones. The resultant products
6b−6j were obtained in good yields. Further, we extended the
scope of an alkyne containing a fragile TIPS group.
Delightfully, the desired product 6k was obtained in 75%
yield. Finally, we varied the aryl group of propargyl sulfides and
obtained the products 6l−6p in good yields (60−86%).
Next, we attempted a few control experiments to gain more
insight into the reaction mechanism. First, we carried out
reactions with benzyl and geranyl phenyl sulfides to differ-
entiate the [2,3]-rearrangement from a probable [1,2]-
rearrangement (Scheme 4a-4b). A reaction of 2a with benzyl
phenyl sulfide 7 did not provide the product 8 under the
optimized conditions that could result via a [1,2]-sigmatropic
rearrangement. In contrast, a reaction with geranyl sulfide 3k
led to 4af, where a shift to the C3-carbon was noticed. This

clearly shows that the [2,3]-rearrangement is involved. Next,
we intend to execute a few control experiments to probe
whether the rearrangement is occurring through a metal-bound
or metal-free sulfur ylide.
20
To investigate it, we executed a few
reactions with 2a and geranyl sulfide 3k with different gold
catalysts (Scheme 4c). The diastereoselectivity of the product
in all of the reactions is found to be 1:1, irrespective of the gold
catalyst and its associated ligands. It concludes that the
rearrangement could occur through a metal-free ylide
intermediate.
5d
Further, to understand the difference in
reactivity of gold and rhodium carbenes with allyl and
propargyl sulfides, we attempted a competitive experiment by
employing 2a and a mixture of 3a and 5a in the presence of
gold/rhodium catalysis (Scheme 4d). We observed that gold
carbenes are more reactive and have better compatibility with
allyl sulfide 3a, as the reaction with AuCl resulted in 4a:6a in
70% yield with a 75:25 ratio. This observation is consistent
with the literature precedent where the gold carbenes showed
better reactivity with allyl sulfides than that of propargyl
sulfides.
5d
While the rhodium carbenes are comparatively less
reactive and have better compatibility with propargyl sulfide,
the reaction with Rh
2
(OAc)
4
provided 4a/6a in a 43:57 ratio
and 63% yield. During our studies, we observed a yellow
coloration upon addition of sulfides to a colorless solution of
AuCl. This could be attributed to a plausible coordination of
sulfide with AuCl. Indeed, it was studied by
1
H NMR and
HRMS analysis.
18
Delightfully, a reaction with the AuCl-
(SMe
2
) catalyst has afforded the product 4a in a comparable
yield (82%, Scheme 4e).
21
It is inferred that allyl sulfide plays a
vital role in the reactions and acts as both the substrate and the
ligand.

We also validated the optimized reaction conditions by
carrying out scale-up reactions for the synthesis of 1,5-enyne
and 1,4-allenyne thioaryl carboxylates (Scheme 5a). Gratify-
ingly, the conditions are compatible, and the desired products
4a and 6a were obtained in 80% and 75% yield, respectively.
Encouraged by the recent research progress in visible-light-
promoted metal-free Doyle−Kirmse reactions,
22
we tried to
synthesize 1,5-enyne and 1,4-allenyne thioaryl carboxylates
under photochemical conditions (Scheme 5b). After a brief
optimization, we observed the products 4a and 6a, however, in
moderate yields.
18
Further, we attempted a few synthetic group transformations
on densely functionalized products 4a/6k (Scheme 6). First,
we carried out functional group interconversions on the
carboxylate group of 4a. The carboxylic acid 9 and alcohol 10
derivatives were obtained after hydrolysis and reduction steps,
respectively. Next, we attempted a hydration of alkynes that
could generate 1,4-dicarbonyl compounds, which are excellent
synthons for numerous transformations. To our delight, we
obtained a highly valuable and functionalized 1,4-dicarbonyl
core 11 in 60% yield upon treating 4a with tosic acid while the
quaternary center remained intact. Surprisingly, the reactions
of 4a with PIFA and I
2
have afforded the respective tri- and
tetrasubstituted alkene cores (12−13) with excellent stereo-
selectivity.
18
Next, a desilylation reaction was executed on 6k
that resulted in the desired product 14 with a versatile terminal
alkyne group.
A tentative mechanism for the transition-metal-catalyzed
Doyle−Kirmse reaction is drawn based on the literature and
our observations (Scheme 7).
5d,20
First, unprotected alkynyl
hydrazone 1 is oxidized to alkynyl diazoacetate 2 under PIDA
promotion. An in situ generated gold-sulfide complex 15
decomposes the diazo compound 2 and forms reactive gold
carbene 16. Next, nucleophilic sulfide 3 adds to the
electrophilic carbene and forms gold-bound ylide 17.
Subsequently, the gold-bound ylide will be stabilized by the
sulfide 3 as in TS1 which could dissociate into free ylide 18
and a gold-sulfide complex.
20c
Finally, ylide 18 undergoes a
facile [2,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement through TS2 that gives
functionalized 1,5-enyne thioaryl carboxylates 4.
In summary, we have shown the first [2,3]-sigmatropic
rearrangement on alkynyl diazoacetate using gold/rhodium
catalysis. The bench-stable alkynyl hydrazones were effectively
employed and delivered 1,5-enyne/1,4-allenyne thioaryl
carboxylates in good to excellent yields. The established
protocol demonstrated a wide substrate scope and good
functional group tolerance. Further, scale-up reactions and
metal-free photochemical synthesis of propargyl sulfide
carboxylates were demonstrated. In addition, the synthetic
utility of the products was demonstrated, which delivered a
functionalized 1,4-dicarbonyl alkene core and other motifs of
interest. Lastly, we evaluated the role of the sulfide in a simple
AuCl catalyzed Doyle−Kirmse reaction and found that sulfide
acts as both ligand and substrate.
